timing_rule: Latest eligible year per source within 3 years; dated fieldwork must end before the decision, otherwise an earlier calendar year is required. Retain all eligible question variants in that year.

photo_id.support_definition: Favoring a general photo-ID requirement; contextual to Indiana’s particular law, not approval of the holding.

cases.name: Crawford v. Marion County Election Board

components.decision: Indiana’s photo-ID requirement remained in place after the Court rejected the facial challenge.
components.scope: The judgment did not establish that every voter-ID law or every application of this law is constitutional.
components.locator: Stevens opinion, Parts III–IV; Scalia concurrence in the judgment; syllabus identifies the separate opinions.
components.survey_fit: The poll asks about photo ID generally. It does not specify Indiana’s exemptions, provisional-ballot process, or burdens on voters who lack qualifying identification.

observations.wording: Should voters have to present official photo identification at the polls on Election Day?
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased question summary. Original question gives a driver’s license as an example. PDF page 47 (printed page 46), Q57, asked all respondents. Nationwide telephone survey of adults, including an oversample in competitive congressional districts; methodology on PDF page 15 and sample/date header on page 20.
observations.weight: Published national topline; no respondent-level recalculation or new weighting.
observations.denominator: All 2,006 adults in the survey, including don’t know/refused responses; not just registered voters. Published percentages retained without normalization.
observations.orientation: Support means favoring a photo-ID requirement.

response_distribution.label: Should not have to do this

cases.interpretation_limit: Six justices agreed on the judgment, not one rationale. Stevens, Roberts and Kennedy relied on the record and the broad challenge; Scalia, Thomas and Alito concurred separately. Souter and Ginsburg dissented, as did Breyer separately. Public policy support does not settle the constitutional question.

limitations: Explicit source-based legal coding is an input, not an automated legal classifier.
Contextual matches do not measure approval of the specific holding.
Mixed and unresolved components retain their labels; no scalar direction is inferred.
No pooling, confidence intervals, causal claims, or prediction.
